title: Special Products and Factorisation — Chapter Summary
intro: Some products of polynomials come up so often that we memorise their expanded forms — the special products. Factorisation reverses the process: given a polynomial, write it as a product of simpler polynomials. The two skills work as a matched pair, and together they let us simplify expressions, perform mental arithmetic and reveal zeros at a glance.

sections.heading: Square of a Binomial
bullets: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 (square-of-sum).
(a − b)^2 = a^2 − 2ab + b^2 (square-of-difference).
Both have the same shape; only the middle sign changes.
Right-hand sides are called perfect-square trinomials.
Common slip: writing (a + b)^2 as a^2 + b^2 — the middle term 2ab is essential.

sections.heading: Difference of Squares and Product-Sum
bullets: (a + b)(a − b) = a^2 − b^2 — middle terms cancel.
Used for clever mental arithmetic: 103 × 97 = (100 + 3)(100 − 3) = 9991.
(x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab.
Coefficient of x is the SUM of the two constants; constant term is the PRODUCT.
Reverse direction (§4.6): factor x^2 + 5x + 6 by finding (a, b) with sum 5 and product 6 — namely (2, 3).

sections.heading: Cubes — Expansion and Factor Identities
bullets: (a − b)^3 = a^3 − 3a^2 b + 3ab^2 − b^3 — signs alternate.
Sum of cubes: a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 − ab + b^2).
Difference of cubes: a^3 − b^3 = (a − b)(a^2 + ab + b^2).

sections.heading: Factorisation — Common Factor and Regrouping
bullets: Step 1 of every factorisation: pull out the greatest common factor.
HCF includes both the numerical and the variable parts.
Example: 12a^2 b − 18ab^2 = 6ab(2a − 3b).
When no factor is common to all, group terms in pairs.
Each pair pulls out its own factor; the resulting parts share a common BINOMIAL factor.

sections.heading: Factorising Quadratic Trinomials
bullets: Type A: x^2 + bx + c — find two numbers with sum b and product c.
Example: x^2 + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) since 2 + 3 = 5 and 2·3 = 6.
Sign pattern: sum negative, product positive → both numbers negative.
Sum positive, product negative → opposite signs (larger one positive).
Type B: ax^2 + bx + c (a ≠ 1) — splitting the middle term.
Find two numbers with sum b and product a·c; split bx into them; regroup.
Example: 3x^2 + 11x + 6 → split 11x = 2x + 9x → (3x + 2)(x + 3).

sections.heading: Recognising Special-Product Patterns in Factorisation
bullets: a^2 − b^2 = (a + b)(a − b) — apply iteratively when possible.
Perfect-square trinomial: a^2 ± 2ab + b^2 = (a ± b)^2.
Sum of cubes: a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 − ab + b^2).
Difference of cubes: a^3 − b^3 = (a − b)(a^2 + ab + b^2).
Strategy: GCF → pattern → split-the-middle → regroup → re-multiply to verify.

key_takeaways: (a ± b)^2 = a^2 ± 2ab + b^2 — middle term is essential.
(a + b)(a − b) = a^2 − b^2 — middle terms cancel.
(x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab — sum and product govern coefficient and constant.
(a ± b)^3 has four terms; a^3 ± b^3 factors using a quadratic factor with the OPPOSITE middle sign.
Always pull out the GCF first when factoring.
Quadratic ax^2 + bx + c factors by splitting bx into two numbers whose sum is b and product is a·c.

glossary.definition: A polynomial product whose expanded form is named and worth memorising, e.g. (a + b)^2.
A trinomial of the form a^2 ± 2ab + b^2 — the expansion of (a ± b)^2.
An expression of the form a^2 − b^2; factors as (a + b)(a − b).
An expression of the form a^3 + b^3; factors as (a + b)(a^2 − ab + b^2).
An expression of the form a^3 − b^3; factors as (a − b)(a^2 + ab + b^2).
The process of writing a polynomial as a product of simpler polynomials.
The largest expression (numerical and variable) that divides every term of a polynomial.
A factoring technique for ax^2 + bx + c: split bx into two terms whose sum is b and product is a·c, then regroup.
A factoring technique that pairs terms so each pair pulls out a matching binomial factor.
For a + b, the conjugate is a − b; their product (a + b)(a − b) is a^2 − b^2.
